How Did One Planet Win a Nobel Prize?

Episode 65 of a daily journey through the universe. 🏆
51 Pegasi b: in 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found the first planet orbiting a Sun-like star, a 'hot Jupiter' with a 4-day year. It won the 2019 Nobel Prize, and opened the door to more than 6,000 confirmed exoplanets.

segments.text: How did one planet win two astronomers a Nobel Prize? It broke all the rules.
In nineteen ninety-five, two Swiss astronomers, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, were watching an ordinary Sun-like star about fifty light-years away.
segments.headline: A Sun-like star

segments.text: The star was wobbling back and forth, ever so slightly. Something big was pulling on it.
segments.headline: A wobbling star

segments.text: It was a planet about half the mass of Jupiter, circling its star in just four days.
That was shocking. In our solar system, giant planets are far from the Sun. This one was closer to its star than Mercury is to ours.
segments.headline: Closer than Mercury

segments.text: Its temperature is about a thousand degrees. Astronomers called this new kind of world a hot Jupiter.
It proved planets around other suns are real, and can be stranger than anything we imagined.
segments.headline: Stranger than imagined

segments.text: In twenty nineteen, Mayor and Queloz won the Nobel Prize in Physics.
segments.headline: Nobel Prize, 2019

segments.text: Since then, the count has exploded. In twenty twenty-five, NASA confirmed more than six thousand exoplanets.
